questions.question: In a constraint-based ZK system, what is the witness?
options: A full assignment to all circuit wires
A list of only the public inputs
The proving key used by the prover
A hash of the source program text
questions.explanation: The witness is the complete set of values (inputs and intermediates) that makes all constraints true.

questions.question: Which shape matches a single R1CS constraint?
options: linear(w) * linear(w) = linear(w)
any polynomial in w equals zero
a boolean clause over input bits
a matrix inverse equals identity
questions.explanation: R1CS constraints multiply two linear combinations and equate them to a third linear combination.

questions.question: Why do fixed-width integers like u32 need extra constraints compared to Field values?
options: They must be range-checked to 32 bits
They require larger field moduli to work
They avoid any need for witness generation
They replace multiplication constraints entirely
questions.explanation: A u32 is a field element plus constraints that force it to lie in the 0..2^32-1 range (and enforce overflow rules).

questions.question: In this lesson's model, what happens for a=2^32-1 and b=1 if you require s=a+b to be u32?
options: The circuit becomes unsatisfied by the witness
The addition wraps around and stays satisfied
The verifier learns the private inputs directly
The compiler deletes the range check as dead code
questions.explanation: The computed sum is 2^32, which fails the 32-bit range constraint, so the witness no longer satisfies the circuit.

questions.question: Why does a compiler often introduce intermediate wires when lowering code to R1CS?
options: Each constraint allows at most one multiplication
R1CS forbids using additions in constraints
R1CS requires every value to be public input
Each constraint must include exactly 64 terms
questions.explanation: Complex expressions are decomposed into single-multiplication steps so they fit the rank-1 form.

questions.question: What is the core risk of unconstrained computation if you forget to constrain its outputs later?
options: A prover can pick any output and still pass
The proof system stops being zero-knowledge
The proving key can be recomputed from inputs
The circuit will always be overconstrained
questions.explanation: If outputs are not tied to inputs by constraints, many different witnesses can satisfy the same circuit.

questions.question: Which pattern correctly makes an unconstrained result safe to use in a proof?
options: Compute outside, then assert a relation inside
Compute outside and return it without checks
Compute inside and avoid using assertions
Compute outside and mark everything as pub
questions.explanation: You can do work unconstrained, but you must add constraints that verify the result matches the intended relation.

questions.question: When a circuit is underconstrained, what can be true for the same public inputs?
options: Multiple different witnesses can satisfy it
Exactly one witness always satisfies it
No witness can ever satisfy any constraint
Only the verifier can choose the witness
questions.explanation: Underconstrained circuits admit multiple valid witnesses for the same instance, which can enable malicious proofs.
